content: Symptomatic patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) in preterm infants is associated with significant risks of mortality and morbidity. Indomethacin, a non-selective cyclooxygenase inhibitor, has shown short-term clinical benefits when used prophylactically in this population. However, its efficacy and safety in treating symptomatic PDA specifically remain unclear. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of indomethacin, administered via any route, compared to placebo or no treatment, in reducing mortality and morbidity in preterm infants with symptomatic PDA. A comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Neonatal standard search strategy. Databases searched included the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Ovid MEDLINE, and CINAHL, with the last search performed on July 31, 2020. Additional searches included clinical trial registries and reference lists of relevant articles to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs. The inclusion criteria were RCTs and quasi-RCTs comparing indomethacin (any dose, any route) to placebo or no treatment in preterm infants. Data collection and analysis followed Cochrane Neonatal's standard methods, with trial quality and data extraction independently assessed by at least two authors. The GRADE approach was used to evaluate the certainty of evidence for key outcomes, including failure of PDA closure within one week, bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) at 28 days and 36 weeks postmenstrual age, need for surgical PDA ligation or transcatheter occlusion, all-cause neonatal mortality, necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), and mucocutaneous or gastrointestinal bleeding. Fourteen RCTs involving 880 preterm infants were included in the analysis. Four of these studies were judged to have a high risk of bias in one or more domains. Indomethacin significantly reduced the risk of failure of PDA closure within one week of the first dose (risk ratio [RR] 0.30, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.23 to 0.38; risk difference [RD] -0.52, 95% CI -0.58 to -0.45; 10 studies, 654 infants; high-certainty evidence). There was little to no difference in the incidence of BPD, whether defined as the need for supplemental oxygen at 28 days postnatal age (RR 1.45, 95% CI 0.60 to 3.51; 1 study, 55 infants; low-certainty evidence) or at 36 weeks postmenstrual age (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.41 to 1.55; 1 study, 92 infants; low-certainty evidence). Similarly, indomethacin likely had little to no effect on all-cause neonatal mortality (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.33; 8 studies, 314 infants; moderate-certainty evidence). No significant differences were observed in the need for surgical PDA ligation (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.33 to 1.29; 7 studies, 275 infants; moderate-certainty evidence), the incidence of NEC (RR 1.27, 95% CI 0.36 to 4.55; 2 studies, 147 infants; low-certainty evidence), or mucocutaneous or gastrointestinal bleeding (RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.01 to 7.58; 2 studies, 119 infants; low-certainty evidence) when comparing indomethacin to placebo or no treatment. The certainty of evidence for BPD, surgical PDA ligation, NEC, and mucocutaneous or gastrointestinal bleeding was downgraded due to serious or very serious imprecision. In conclusion, high-certainty evidence supports the efficacy of indomethacin in closing symptomatic PDA in preterm infants compared to placebo or no treatment. However, evidence regarding its effects on other clinically relevant outcomes and potential adverse effects remains insufficient.
